questions.q: Which mental model does the lesson recommend for thinking about an AI assistant?
options: A search engine that looks up verified answers on the web
A brilliant new assistant on their first day who has never met you
A thinking mind that already knows your preferences and goals
A database of checked facts that is almost never wrong
questions.explain: The lesson pictures AI as a brilliant, well-read new assistant on their first day: fast and knowledgeable, but it doesn't know you and can be confidently wrong.

questions.q: You typed "Give me dinner ideas." and got a generic list. What would most improve the next answer?
options: Send the exact same request again in a fresh chat
Cut it down to a few keywords, like a search box
Accept the list, since the first reply is the finished product
Add who's eating, your time, your budget and what to avoid
questions.explain: The lesson's improved dinner prompt briefs the assistant on who's eating, time, budget and dislikes, because better context in means better answers out.

questions.q: You have a page of messy meeting notes and want them turned into a tidy checklist. Is this a good job for an AI assistant?
options: Yes, organizing words into lists is a language task it does well
No, it can only give answers stored in a database of facts
Only if it first searches the web for similar checklists
No, it works best when you type just a few short keywords
questions.explain: Organizing messy notes into lists, plans and checklists is one of the language tasks the lesson says AI is great at.
